Another Claude session sent a message:
<cross-session-message from="uds:/tmp/cc-socks/5789.sock" from-name="Tlog stream deprecation notice" from-mode="prompting">
Handover for **COR-1226 — "Correct Datadog severity mapping for Go slog error logs"**, from the session that just closed COR-1223 (NATS 2.14.4 fleet upgrade). I confirmed the symptom live and found the mechanism, so you shouldn't need to re-derive any of this.

Ticket: https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1226 · INC-49 follow-up · currently unassigned, Backlog.

## The bug, and it's still live as of 2026-08-10 16:17Z

Datadog indexes Go service logs as `status:info` regardless of actual severity, so any monitor filtering `status:error` is structurally incapable of firing. Confirmed against `kube_namespace:mirror-worker`, 364 matching lines in 4h, all 19 sampled show the same thing:

```
message: 2026/08/10 16:10:46 WARN Permanent sync error, terminating
         error="sync: list source refs: ... http 404 ... Repository not found."
status:  info          <- should be warn
custom.status: ""      <- empty string
```

Not one line was correctly classified.

## Mechanism — two compounding causes, NOT a simple remapper

**1. slog is using the TEXT handler, not JSON.** Severity is embedded inside the message string (`... 16:10:46 WARN Permanent sync error ...`), so there is no structured `level` attribute to remap. I queried `@level:ERROR` first and got **zero** results — that field does not exist. Don't waste time on a status remapper keyed to `level`; there's nothing to key on.

**2. Logs arrive via OTLP, not the Datadog agent file tailer.** Tags on every line: `source:otlp_log_ingestion`, `otel_source:datadog_exporter`. `custom.status` comes through as an empty string and Datadog falls back to `info`.

So there's a real fork in the road, and it's a design decision rather than a config tweak:
- switch services to slog's **JSON handler** so severity becomes structured, then remap (cleanest, touches every Go service)
- fix severity at the **OTel collector** so OTLP `SeverityNumber` / status is populated (one place, no service changes — probably the best lead)
- **grok/category processor** parsing the level back out of message text (ugliest, no service changes, works today)

## Where pipeline code lives

`catalog/modules/datadog-cloudflare-logs-pipeline/` in `entirehq/infra` is the working precedent — `datadog_logs_custom_pipeline` with `category_processor` → scratch field → status remap, and its comments explain the first-match ordering. Copy that shape.

There is **no equivalent module for Go/k8s logs**. I searched the whole infra repo for `status_remapper` and `logs_pipeline`: zero hits outside that Cloudflare module. So you're creating something new, not editing something existing.

Fleet-side, the OTel collector docs are `docs/operator-guide/otel-collector.md` (gateway + agent architecture, enrichment processors, filter rationale) — that's where option 2 would land.

## The second half of the ticket: reviewing status:error monitors

43 matches for `status:error` in `entirehq/infra`. Needs filtering before you trust the number — some are APM/trace queries where `status:error` is a span attribute and works correctly, and some are docs/dashboards. The real candidates are LOG monitors on GO services:
- `catalog/modules/datadog-entire-core/` — monitor_oauth_errors, monitor_token_errors, monitor_nats_consumer_errors, monitor_perms_sweep_error_logs, monitor_spicedb_permission_errors, monitor_request_error_rate
- `catalog/modules/datadog-entiredb-health-fleet/` — monitor_fsck_errors, monitor_diss_errors, monitor_taskloop_errors, monitor_admin_grpc_errors
- `catalog/modules/datadog-entire-mcp/` — monitor_request_errors, monitor_token_exchange_errors
- `catalog/modules/datadog-marvin-health/stream_text_errors.tf`, `datadog-search/`, `datadog-ai-gateway-health/monitor_errors.tf`

The uncomfortable framing worth putting in the ticket: **those monitors are green today because they match nothing.**

## Do NOT break the existing workaround

Every monitor that currently works matches literal message text, never status. Examples verified live in Datadog:
- `[k8s] NATS JetStream stream wedged — cannot write, PAGE (prod)` id 309685807 → `logs("... \"is not current: stream write error\"")`
- `[k8s] NATS config reload rejected (prod)` id 305465599 → `logs("... \"Failed to reload server configuration\"")`

These keep working after your fix; they just stop being the only option. Don't "modernise" them to `status:error` in the same change — that couples a working detection path to an unproven one.

## Related gotcha in the same family (already fixed, but instructive)

Datadog auto-injects its own `priority:pN` tag, which won `$TAGS[priority]` and meant **no Datadog alert could page or be silenced at all** until 2026-07-30. Fix was infra#1009, renaming the tier tag to `alert_tier:`. Writeup in `catalog/modules/datadog-incident-io-webhook/main.tf`, routing table in `incident-io/README.md`. Same root pattern as your bug: Datadog silently overriding a user-supplied field. Expect more.

## Verification advice — this is the part I'd insist on

Verify by confirming a known ERROR line actually indexes as `status:error`. Do **not** verify by "the monitor fires" or "the pipeline applied". A filter that matches nothing is indistinguishable from a clean result, and that is precisely the bug you are fixing — it would be easy to ship a fix and confirm it with a check that couldn't fail.

I hit that trap three times in one session today: a kubectl label selector matching no pods (reported 0 errors, examined nothing), `grep -c` on single-line output returning 1 regardless of match count, and grepping `permissions violation` when NATS actually logs `Publish Violation`. The last one nearly buried a real ACL bug (COR-1224). I wrote the general trap into `docs/runbooks/nats-server-upgrade.md` §3a in the fleet repo if you want the phrasing.

## Why this matters more than its priority suggests

INC-49: 50,899 failure logs indexed as info. From the incident Slack writeup — *"Every status:error monitor on our Go services cannot fire — Datadog indexes slog ERROR as status:info. Currently untracked. This is half of why today took 97 minutes."* nats-server had been logging the exact fault since its second minute; responders reached that diagnosis 52 minutes later.

It also constrains other INC-49 work: any new log-based monitor must match on message text until this is fixed. COR-1102's sticky-write alert was written that way deliberately for this reason.

## Context you may want

- COR-1223 (NATS 2.14.4) closed today, all 7 clusters upgraded. COR-1224 (webhooks_github_v1 $JS.ACK grants) fixed and merged. COR-1225 and COR-1227 closed as duplicates of already-shipped work (COR-1102 and COR-1088).
- INC-49 has 3 outstanding follow-ups after that: COR-1087 (shrink webhook NATS messages), COR-1091 (document GitHub App credentials), and yours.
- Note for prod cluster access: the plain prod kubectl contexts cannot `create pods/portforward` — use the `-admin` variants. The failure looks like `HTTP 000` / a bad URL rather than an RBAC denial, which cost me time.

Ask if you want anything I dug up in more detail — I still have the session context.
</cross-session-message>

Also worth noting the handover missed the entire `catalog/modules/datadog-mirror-pipeline/` module — 40 monitors on these exact services, all metric or span based, **zero log alerts**. input.description:
Follow-up from COR-1226. Now that mirror-pipeline severity actually reaches Datadog, the dominant source of `status:error` volume on these services is transient NATS reconnect noise, not real faults.

## Evidence

During the COR-1223 NATS 2.14.4 rolling upgrade on 2026-08-10, `eks-prod-us-east-2` produced **161 ERROR-level lines in a single 5-minute window** from mirror-pipeline alone. Sampled patterns, all in 15:02–15:05Z:

| count | service | line |
|---|---|---|
| 15 | meta-fanout | `ERROR Fetch error error="nats: disconnected during fetch"` |
| 15 | meta-fanout | `ERROR Fetch error error="nats: Leadership Changed"` |
| 14 | fanout | `ERROR Fetch error error="nats: disconnected during fetch"` |
| 14 | trails-fanout | `ERROR Fetch error error="nats: disconnected during fetch"` |
| 12 | fanout | `ERROR Fetch error error="nats: Leadership Changed"` |
| 7 | fanout / trails-fanout | `ERROR nuts: NATS disconnected conn="" error=EOF` |

These are the expected consequence of a rolling restart — the client reconnects and continues. Nothing is lost and no operator action is warranted, but they are emitted at ERROR.

## Why it matters

`[k8s] Application error log surge` fires above 50 errors / 5 min / cluster (`aws/entire-prod/datadog/platform-observability/terragrunt.hcl`). 161 is over 3× that. It is tagged `alert_tier:notice`, so it posts to the FYI feed rather than paging — a nuisance, not an incident — but it will recur on every NATS restart and it dilutes the signal the monitor exists to carry.

None of the four current `error_log_exclude_msgs` entries match these lines; they are all entire-core phrases.

## Suggested direction

Re-level rather than suppress. A disconnect that the client recovers from is a WARN; reserve ERROR for a reconnect that exhausts its budget or a fetch that fails terminally. Two emitters are involved:

- `github.com/entireio/go-nuts` — the `nuts: NATS disconnected` line
- `mirror-pipeline` — `Fetch error`, `Lifecycle fetch error`, `Subscribe failed` in the fanout consumers

If re-leveling is not wanted, the fallback is adding `Fetch error` / `NATS disconnected` to `error_log_exclude_msgs`. That is strictly worse: it blinds the fleet monitor to those phrases for every service, and after COR-1226 the free-text match lands on the slog `msg` only, so it would suppress genuine fetch failures too.

## Not urgent

Nothing is broken. This is signal hygiene that only became visible because COR-1226 made severity honest.

Fixes COR-1226. Go slog ERROR/WARN lines from every mirror-pipeline service were indexed by Datadog as status:info, so status:error log queries and monitors could not see them. 464 ERROR and 221,700 WARN lines in the 24h before this change.
Cause
None of the binaries installed a slog handler, so they fell through to slog's built-in default, which writes via the standard log package:
2026/08/10 16:10:46 ERROR Permanent sync error, terminating error="..."
The fleet's OTel collector agent derives severity from the log line itself (fleet/infrastructure/controllers/otel-collector/helmrelease-agent.yaml:67-90) — a json_parser mapping a top-level level field, with a regex_parser fallback for logfmt level=ERROR. That format matches neither, so severity stayed UNSPECIFIED and Datadog fell back to info.
This is scoped to this repo. entire-api, entiredb, and the rest already install JSON handlers and classify correctly in prod today; no collector or Datadog pipeline change is needed.

New internal/slogutil, installed from each of the 8 service mains alongside the existing otelsetup.Setup call. Mirrors entiredb/slogutil and entire-api/internal/slogutil. No new dependencies.
Two deliberate differences from those two packages, both documented in the package comment:
No service attribute. The service tag comes from the collector's transform/service-name processor via the pod's app label, and cmd/rekicker reports itself to OTel as mirror-rekicker while its pods are rekicker. Emitting our own risks re-tagging a live service out from under existing dashboards and monitors.
Terminal output stays logfmt rather than pulling in tint/isatty. It is still severity-parseable by the collector's regex fallback, so the two paths cannot disagree about a line's severity.
Output moves from stderr to stdout, matching the sibling repos. Both streams are tailed by the filelog receiver, so this changes nothing about which lines are collected.

input.title: Rename reserved `status` slog attributes in entire-api and entiredb
input.description:
Extends the COR-1226 fix to `entire-api` and `entiredb`. Found while verifying COR-1226 in prod; fixed for `mirror-pipeline` in [trail #95](https://entire.io/gh/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/trails/95).

## The defect

An slog attribute literally named `status` is lifted out of the JSON body by the OTel collector's `json_parser` and written into Datadog's **reserved** status field. The status remapper then reads it as the record's severity, and a value it cannot parse as one — an HTTP status code, a job state — silently degrades the record to `status:info`, discarding the OTLP SeverityNumber the collector derived from `level`.

Nothing errors. The log line still arrives. It just lands at the wrong severity, which is the same invisibility that let COR-1226 survive until INC-49.

## Evidence

Org-wide over 7 days, **every** log carrying an app `status` of 400/401/403/404/409/500/502/503 indexed as `info` — roughly 28k lines. Top contributors, all owned by these two repos:

| service | @status | count | repo |
|---|---|---|---|
| entire-core-regional-us | 400 | 8,005 | entiredb |
| entire-api | 404 | 5,003 | entire-api |
| entire-core-regional-us | 404 | 4,572 | entiredb |
| entire-api | 503 | 2,819 | entire-api |
| entire-core-regional-eu | 404 | 1,575 | entiredb |
| entire-api | 403 | 956 | entire-api |
| entire-api | 502 | 874 | entire-api |
| entire-api | 500 | 480 | entire-api |

These are services that emit genuine `status:error` on their *other* lines, so this is not a service-wide misconfiguration — it is per-line suppression, only on lines carrying the attribute.

Unlike mirror-pipeline, both repos have always installed JSON handlers, so this has been suppressing severity for as long as those call sites have existed. It is independent of COR-1226 and was not caused by it.

## Call sites

`entire-api` — 7 occurrences across 6 files:

* `internal/httpapi/errors.go:67` — **error path**
* `internal/httpapi/observability.go:240`
* `internal/gateway/proxy/proxy.go:157`
* `internal/ingest/checkpoint_repo.go:155`
* `internal/runner/consumer.go:740`, `internal/runner/handlers.go:600`, `:832`

`entiredb` — 22 occurrences across 15 files, several at error level:

* `core/coreapi/ci_webhooks.go:849`, `:854` — **`slogutil.Error`**
* `core/coreapi/org_ci_webhooks.go:296`, `:301` — **`slogutil.Error`**
* `internal/ciwebhooks/dispatcher/dispatcher.go:425` — **`slogutil.Error`**, also `:401`
* `core/api/json.go:20`, `core/api/middleware.go:594`, `core/api/server.go:2359`, `core/api/autherror.go:148`, `core/api/client.go:106`, `core/api/admin_repo_cell_state.go:142`
* `core/authn/cimd/fetch.go:135`, `:158`, `core/authn/github_provider.go:95`
* `internal/entirecore/mirrordone/consumer.go:219`, `:247`, `internal/entirecore/mirrordone/composite.go:76`
* `internal/entirecore/account_deletion_reaper_runonce.go:127`
* `cmd/entire-deploy/datadog/datadog.go:185`

Also in `entiredb`, 3 occurrences of `slog.String("msg", ...)` — same class, collides with the message body:

* `slogutil/memberlist_log.go:26`, `internal/entirecore/account_deletion_reaper_runonce.go:127`, plus one more

## Suggested change

Mirror what landed in mirror-pipeline:

* HTTP codes → `http.status_code` (Datadog's standard facet, and the usual semantic twin of the `http.response.status_code` span attribute)
* Domain states → a namespaced key, e.g. `mirror.status`
* `msg` → `detail` or similar

Then port the AST guard test from `mirror-pipeline/internal/slogutil/reserved_attrs_test.go`. It walks the module and fails on any Datadog-reserved slog attribute key, covering both typed constructors and the implicit `slog.Info(msg, "status", v)` / `logger.With(...)` forms. Without it this reappears the next time someone logs an HTTP status, and nothing will indicate that it has.

Note `entiredb` uses `slogutil.Error(ctx, msg, attrs...)` wrappers, so the ported test needs those call shapes added to its selector table.

## Explicitly not in scope

`source`, `trace_id`, `span_id`, and `service` are all reserved in Datadog's docs but verified fine on this path:

* `source` lands as a plain `custom.source` attribute with the `source:otlp_log_ingestion` tag intact
* `trace_id` / `span_id` in both repos' `slogctx.go` are deliberate and are what drives trace correlation
* `service` in both `slogutil` packages matches the collector-derived service tag

Only `status` (and `msg`) need changing.

## Observed live — and it fires more often than this ticket says

`[k8s] Application error log surge (prod)` triggered at P3 on `eks-prod-ap-south-1` shortly after COR-1226 went live.

Cause was **our own deploy**, not a NATS restart. The trail #94 run completed 17:18:32Z and the mirror-pipeline pods rolled:

| minute | service | errors |
|---|---|---|
| 17:17 | fanout | 36 |
| 17:18 | mirror-worker | 58 |

94 in one 5-minute bucket against a threshold of 50. Every line was `nats: no responders available for request`, plus one `Failed to subscribe` / `context deadline exceeded` and two `Lifecycle fetch error` / `nats: consumer deleted`. Each burst spanned **~80 milliseconds** — 57 errors between 17:18:38.658 and 17:18:38.741 — which is the shape of every in-flight fetch on a pod failing at once as it shuts down, not a fault.

Fully self-recovered. Nothing since beyond the normal 1–2/min entire-api background.

## Correction to the description above

I wrote that this would recur "on every NATS restart." That understates the frequency: a rolling pod restart produces it just as readily, so it fires on **every mirror-pipeline deploy** — a far more common event than a NATS upgrade. Any deploy touching the fanout services or mirror-worker will trip the cluster surge monitor from now on.

That makes the case for re-leveling stronger than originally written. A consumer whose fetch is interrupted by its own graceful shutdown is not an error condition; it is the expected path through `SIGTERM`. Reserving ERROR for fetches that fail outside shutdown — or that exhaust their retry budget — would remove the whole class without suppressing anything real.

Worth noting the alternative gets worse with this evidence too: excluding the phrase `Fetch error` fleet-wide would blind the monitor to genuine fetch failures on every service, and those bursts are exactly what a real JetStream problem looks like.

content.text:
Here's what I found — the diagnosis is sharper than "log at WARN".

There's **already** a shutdown guard, `nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr(ctx, err)` from COR-923, called at every one of the 8 sites. It didn't fire because it's too narrow:

```go
func IsShutdownFetchErr(ctx context.Context, err error) bool {
	return ctx.Err() != nil &&
		(errors.Is(err, nats.ErrConnectionClosed) || errors.Is(err, nats.ErrConnectionDraining))
}
```

It covers two error values. The bursts were overwhelmingly `nats: ErrNoResponders` — plus `consumer deleted` and `context deadline exceeded`. So the concept was right and the predicate just has holes.

But there are really **two** scenarios, and only one is a shutdown:

1. **Our pod rolling** (today's bursts) — `ctx` *is* cancelled. Widening the predicate fixes this.
2. **NATS server rolling while we run** (the COR-1223 burst at 15:02) — `ctx` is live, so `IsShutdownFetchErr` can *never* help. These need classifying as transient link-loss.

Both tripped the monitor, so fixing only the first would leave you alerting on every NATS upgrade. My suggestion covers both:

- `ctx` done + connection closed/draining/no-responders → **Debug**, clean return (widen the existing predicate)
- `ctx` live + known link-loss (no-responders, disconnected, leadership changed, timeout) → **Warn**; the outer loop already resubscribes with backoff, so this is a recoverable event, not a fault
- anything unrecognised → stays **Error**

That empties `status:error` of restart noise without suppressing a phrase or blinding the monitor.

git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
Recognise the rest of the transient pull-consumer failures

IsShutdownFetchErr matched only ErrConnectionClosed and ErrConnectionDraining,
but a real drain rarely ends on one of those. A rolling pod restart mostly
produces ErrNoResponders, and a NATS server upgrade produces
ErrFetchDisconnected and ErrConsumerLeadershipChanged. Callers gated their
error log on the predicate, so every one of those was logged as a fault.

Measured on one mirror-pipeline deploy: a single pod emitted 57 ErrNoResponders
inside 83 milliseconds as its in-flight fetches failed together, and two
services between them crossed a cluster's error-log alert threshold three times
in forty minutes. The alerts were correct about the count and wrong about the
meaning, which is the failure mode that teaches operators to skim the one
signal that should mean something (COR-1226 / COR-1228).

Split the judgement in two. IsTransientFetchErr answers "is this recoverable",
independent of shutdown — a server rolling underneath a healthy caller produces
these while ctx is still live, so no ctx-based predicate can classify them.
IsShutdownFetchErr becomes exactly "transient AND ctx done", which widens it
correctly and leaves one list to maintain instead of two overlapping ones. A
test pins that relationship so the predicates cannot drift apart again.

ErrTimeout stays out: an idle poll reaching MaxWait is the steady state of a
quiet consumer, and callers already continue on it. context.DeadlineExceeded
stays out too — a slow server and a wedged one raise the same error, so
swallowing it would hide real stalls.

Callers should now log transient-but-running below error level and keep
looping, reserving error for failures that stop recovering.
